name: Roth's Gugu Warra
sweep_summary: The only title hit for gugu1256 (Milojkovic 2013, 'semantic prosody' in corpus stylistics) is a Glottolog computerized language code mis-assignment from the title word 'improvement' (verbatim in the Glottolog record; it has nothing to do with this language or word stress. No first-hand stress statement for Roth's Gugu Warra was found: the prior check pass in the same directory had already established that the language is known only from Roth's 1898 wordlist and Sommer 1976/1999 notes, with the only Lamalamic stress remarks (Verstraete 2023 OGAL ch. 72: vowel-initial roots stressed on the second syllable) pertaining to Rimanggudinhma (mbar1253), not Roth's doculect. The language is not in the catalog; nothing to confirm or contradict. for the session was exhausted (2000/2000), so no additional searches were run; direct download and automated download were used for the Glottolog record.

earlier_scan.note: Only wordlist-level records (Roth 1898, Sommer 1976); no phonological description exists

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. 1969. Three Lamalamic languages of North Queensland. In Papers in Australian Linguistics No. 4, 71-97. Pacific Linguistics A-17. Canberra: ANU. [A's work 7, re-reported because A missed its stress paragraph]
sources.note: For the three Lamalamic languages jointly: stress may be contrastive (two Parimankutinma forms cited) but is overwhelmingly on the first consonant-initial syllable (so initial in C-initial words, second in the many V-initial words); stress is written only when it deviates. p.77: Umbuygamu geminates may be conditioned by 'the very heavy stress on the following syllable'; 'All unstressed vowels in Lamalamic languages tend towards [a]'.

sources.citation: Verstraete, Jean-Christophe. 2019 [online 2017]. Umbuygamu. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 49(2) (Illustrations of the IPA), c. pp.245-264. doi 10.1017/S0025100317000172
sources.note: Section 'Stress and word structure': stress judged by the (non-native) author, assumed cued by the primary pitch movement; vowel-initial roots (about two-thirds of the lexicon) are stressed on the second syllable, consonant-initial roots on the first; compounds carry stress on the stressable syllable of the second root; post-tonic vowel centralisation corroborates.

sources.citation: Dryer, Matthew S. & Martin Haspelmath (eds). 2013. WALS Online (v2020+). Leipzig: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology. [Features 14A 'Fixed Stress Locations', 15A 'weight-sensitive Stress', 16A 'Weight Factors in weight-sensitive Stress Systems', 17A 'Rhythm Types', by Rob Goedemans & Harry van der Hulst; datapoints for Anguthimri (agt), Lamu-Lamu (lla), Uradhi (uhi)]

sources.note: 14A = Second; 15A = Fixed stress (no weight-sensitivity); 16A = No weight; source Laycock 1971 [=1969].
